Why abstract

Abstract art changes the game.

In a classroom, a child with learning differences meets a right answer they cannot reach. In abstract art there is no correct final image at all. Take away the failure, and what is left is sensory exploration, personal voice, and real developmental work.

Fine motor strength

Hands and shoulders

Sweeping brushstrokes, gripping a range of tools, moulding and pressing texture. Hand strength, bilateral coordination and dexterity all build here, without the fatigue and dread of handwriting drills.

Mood and regulation

A place to put it

Art is a language that needs no words. Rhythm, colour and fluid movement give a child somewhere to send a big feeling, and a way to settle themselves and grow their tolerance for frustration.

Executive function

Plan, choose, adapt

Plan a stroke. Choose a medium. Then adapt when the canvas does something you did not expect. That loop, run every week, is the same one a child needs for homework, packing a bag and getting through a school day.

Growth mindset

No mistakes here

In this studio there are no mistakes, only unexpected design choices. Reframing a spill as a decision is how perfectionism loosens its grip, and how a child who is anxious about school starts taking risks again.

A tailored, sensory-friendly journey.

Every session is built to be accessible, safe and worth finishing. The point is not that a child copes with the room. It is that the room was made for them in the first place.

Adaptable pacingNobody is timed. A child who takes three weeks over one piece has not fallen behind.
Room to explore aloneReal choices with real consequences: the surface, the palette, whether to keep going or stop.
Sensory-friendly materialsTextures, smells and tools chosen with sensitivities in mind, and a quiet corner that is always open.
Two adults, alwaysAn exhibiting artist and a Lodestone learning specialist, together, every single session.
Three groups

The same paint.
Three very different jobs.

A four-year-old needs their whole arm moving and no picture to make. A fourteen-year-old needs a body of work and a wall to hang it on. Same studio, same materials, three different jobs to do.

Ages 4 – 6

Splash

Whole-body mark-making. Hands, sponges, rollers and big paper on the floor and on the wall. Nothing here is a picture of anything, and nothing is meant to be. The doing is the point.

Builds: shoulder and whole-arm movement, two hands working together, and a first sense of how hard to press.

Ends with: a folder of everything they made, and one piece chosen for the studio wall.

Ages 7 – 10

Layers

Building a painting up instead of getting it right first time. Wet on wet, wax resist, printing, palette knife, collage over paint. Every session adds something to what was already there.

Builds: grip and control of smaller tools, pressure and pace, and choosing a colour on purpose rather than by accident.

Ends with: one finished piece on canvas, framed and hung in the term show.

Ages 11 – 15

Series

One personal theme carried across three or more works. Acrylic on canvas, scale and composition, and the vocabulary to say what a piece is doing. Closer to a working studio than a class.

Builds: sustained attention across weeks, self-critique, and speaking about their own work to someone else.

Ends with: hanging their own series in the exhibition, with a title card and a statement they wrote.

Inside the studio

Real hands, real paint, real mess.

The artist

Parames McNeill

Abstract painter · Art N Exploration

Her own work is predominantly abstract, made across a wide range of materials and processes, and she describes her method as letting a free spirit lead. It has shown at KLCC, Gallery Kayangan and the Royal Selangor Club, and is collected internationally through The Arabian Gallery in Dubai.

Since 2014 she has taught with My Shining Star Foundation, SOLS 24/7, the National Cancer Society, and GOLD, an organisation working with people with learning disabilities. Her own programme runs on one idea: that anyone can paint freely from whatever level they start at.

Ask about a place

A free 15-minute call first, then one trial session before you commit.

  • Two adults in every session, an exhibiting artist and a learning specialist.
  • Eight children maximum, at the same 1:4 ratio as every Lodestone programme.
  • A plan for your child, reviewed monthly against what we see in the room.
  • All materials supplied, from clay and canvas to the aprons.
  • A kept portfolio, a review each term, and a place in the exhibition.
  • No diagnosis required, and no report needed to enrol.
Is this art therapy?

No, and we are careful with the word. CanvasQuest is an art-based developmental programme taught by an artist and a learning specialist. It is not delivered by a registered art therapist and it is not a clinical service.

Is this suitable for a child with dysgraphia, ADHD or autism?

Yes. The class is built around children with dysgraphia, dyspraxia, ADHD, autism and dyslexia, and it is open to every child alongside them. No diagnosis and no report is needed to enrol. On the first call we ask what already helps your child and what does not, and we plan the term around that.

Is it only abstract art?

Abstract is where we start, because it removes the fear of getting it wrong. As children gain confidence, and particularly in the 11 to 15 group, real technique on canvas comes in alongside it.

My child says they are terrible at art.

That sentence is usually the reason to come. Nothing here is marked or corrected, and the materials are chosen so the first thing they make is something they want to take home.

Will it help their handwriting?

It builds the shoulder stability, wrist position, coordination, pressure control and confidence that handwriting sits on top of. We will not promise legible handwriting in twelve weeks, and you should be wary of anyone who does.

My child is not neurodivergent. Can they still join?

Yes, and the room is better for the mix. The design simply means no child is ever the one being accommodated.
